meta.title: Research | Abdullah
meta.description: Research interests and projects by Abdullah Al Bashit

projects.title: Donor and Treatment Choice in Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation
description: Allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation can cure leukemia, because the donor's immune cells attack the remaining cancer. The donor cells can also attack the patient's own tissues. Apart from relapse, this complication, graft-versus-host disease (GvHD), causes the most deaths after transplant. To lower that risk, donor selection guidelines rank donors mainly by human leukocyte antigen (HLA) match and donor age. Such a ranking gives no estimate of how a given patient will fare with a given donor and treatment.

In MATCH (Artificial Intelligence for Donor Matching), an ARPA-H project with the NMDP, we build models that estimate a patient's outcomes under a given donor and treatment. The models learn from past transplants in the registry of the Center for International Blood and Marrow Transplant Research (CIBMTR). From the registry records, a deep time-to-event network estimates the risks of GvHD, relapse and death, and it updates the risks as events occur after transplant. We also estimate treatment effects from the registry data and test the estimates against randomized trials. We aim to give clinicians a tool that compares a patient's likely outcomes across donors and treatments.

projects.title: Aging Pathway Curation for Multi-omic Assays
description: Drugs that slow aging take many years to test, because a trial must wait for differences in age-related disease or death. Biomarkers that respond to a drug within months could shorten such trials. FAST (Finding Aging Biomarkers by Searching Existing Trials), an ARPA-H project led by Columbia University, searches for such biomarkers in stored blood samples from completed trials. In the samples, six assay platforms measure proteins, metabolites and DNA methylation.

To interpret the measurements as aging biology, we find the assays that relate to canonical aging pathways. Evidence for the pathways comes from the Human Aging Atlas, which gathers aging associations from six independent published sources. We keep a pathway from the Reactome database only when at least two of the sources support it, so that no single dataset decides which pathways count as aging pathways. We then link the proteins, metabolites and CpG probes on the six platforms to the canonical aging pathways through standard identifiers (UniProt, ChEBI and the nearby gene). The resulting curated aging pathways list the FAST assays that measure the pathway members.

projects.title: Structural Characterization of Pathological Inclusions in Alzheimer's Disease
description: In Alzheimer's disease, the proteins amyloid-β (Aβ) and tau aggregate into fibrils. One protein can fold into more than one fibril form, and the forms may damage tissue differently. Current methods cannot measure fibril structure where the fibrils sit, because PET and MRI image the brain far too coarsely, and cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and solid-state NMR resolve fibrils only after purification from tissue.

Scanning X-ray microdiffraction measures fibril structure inside thin sections of tissue, because a synchrotron X-ray beam a few micrometers wide records a diffraction pattern at successive points of the section. The surrounding tissue scatters far more strongly than the fibrils, so the fibril signal stays weak. With neuropathologists at Massachusetts General Hospital and biophysicists at Brookhaven National Laboratory, we develop statistical signal processing and machine learning methods that separate the fibril signal from the tissue background and classify the patterns as Aβ, tau or tissue. We aim to identify which fibril forms appear as tissue degenerates, so that future treatments could target those forms.

projects.title: Multi-omic Risk Stratification in Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
description: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) narrows the airways and destroys the walls of the air sacs (emphysema), and it ranks among the leading causes of death worldwide. Clinicians assess the disease with whole-lung measures, such as spirometry and a CT score of total emphysema, so they see neither the failing lung region nor the biological process behind the damage.

We link molecular measurements in blood to damage in specific lung regions, so that a blood test can point to both the process and the region. The data come from the COPDGene study, which follows current and former smokers for about ten years with chest CT, blood RNA sequencing and plasma proteomics. Co-expression network analysis groups genes and proteins into modules, which we relate to emphysema in lung regions defined on CT. A high-dimensional causal mediation model then tests which plasma proteins carry the effect of smoking on emphysema progression. From those proteins, we develop a multi-omic risk score that ranks patients by risk of lung-function decline and death.
